This article describes the methods to plot the spacial data underlying postcodElapse. To enable spatial plotting in R, installation of of the R packages [tidyverse](https://tidyverse.org/),
[tidyterra](https://dieghernan.github.io/tidyterra/articles/tidyterra.html) and
[ggpubr](https://rpkgs.datanovia.com/ggpubr/) is required.

## Automatic plotting
PostcodElapse provides `plotElapse()` to automatically build ggplot2 figures. The function provides a set of arguments to make standard plots of the spatial data involved in postcodElapse.

### ELAPSE

First, plot a map with the spatial relations of the postal codes. In postcodElapse, ELAPSE is used, which can be loaded and plotted as indicated below:

```{r autoplot ELAPSE}
library(ggpubr)
library(postcodElapse)

plotElapse()
```

ELAPSE has multiple layers to plot a specific one first load ELAPSE with `loadElapse()`. Subsequently provide a specific layer to `plotElapse()` via sub-setting. (the `$` operator)

```{r autoplot ELAPSE one-layer}
elapse <- loadElapse()

plotElapse(elapse = elapse$NO2FULL)
```

## Postal coded geo-locations

To plot the location of postcodes on ELAPSE provide postal addresses to the `postcodes` argument of `plotElapse()`. Additional provide a corresponding GeoPackage to the `BAG_gpkg` and `PC6_gpkg` arguments, see the block below.

```{r autoplot Layers}
data("oneHunderdAddresses")

plotElapse(postcodes = oneHunderdAddresses,
           BAG_gpkg = "../../../data/bag-light.gpkg")
```

Providing both GeoPackages will result in a single figure with both layers plotted.

## Zooming and annotating

The scale of ELAPSE prohibits the visualization of the data. To alleviate this, the `zoom_postcodes` and `annotate_postcodes` arguments are provided. Annotating draws a rectangle around the given postal addresses. And zoom scales the figure axist to zoom into a the given postal address. See the example below on how to build an inset figure with both of these features.

Pass a postal address to either and annotate or zoom into that postal address. Important note zooming and annotating are **mutually exclusive**.


```{r autoplot Annotate and Zoom}
main <- plotElapse(postcodes = oneHunderdAddresses,
                   BAG_gpkg = "../../../data/bag-light.gpkg",
                   PC6_gpkg = "../../../data/cbs_pc6_2024.gpkg",
                   annotate_postcodes = "9947PB", # Zoom into this postcode
                   no_facet = TRUE # Don't add facet_wrap()
                   )

inset <- plotElapse(postcodes = oneHunderdAddresses,
                    BAG_gpkg = "../../../data/bag-light.gpkg",
                    PC6_gpkg = "../../../data/cbs_pc6_2024.gpkg",
                    zoom_postcodes = "9947PB", # Annotate this postcode
                    no_facet = TRUE
                    )

ggarrange(main, inset, ncol = 2) # Put then together
```

Additionally `colour, fill, alpha and size` arguments are provided to customize some aspects of the figures. With this material you can utilize the built-in plotting postcodElapse provides. If you wish to take full control over plotting continue the article below.

## Full control
In this section walks trough the same concepts discussed in the "Automatic plotting" chapter just replacing `autoPlot()` with ggplot2 and postcodElapse.

### ELAPSE
To plot ELAPSE load it and provide it to the `data` argument of an `geom_spatraster()`. The pollution concentrations extracted from ELAPSE are mapped to *fill* we recommend, scaling the colour with `scale_fill_grass_c()`
```{r raw ELAPSE}
library(postcodElapse)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggpubr)

elapse <- loadElapse()

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse) +
  scale_fill_grass_c() +
  facet_wrap(~lyr)
```

Plotting a single layer can be achieved trough sub-setting ELAPSE with the `$` operator.

### Accessing postal coded geo-locations
To plot the location of postal addresses on ELAPSE the corresponding spacial data is required, this is provided trough: `pollutionFromBag()` and `pollutionFromPc6()` functions. These functions return spacial data in the *geom* column. Plotting this data is done using `goem_sf()`, see the block below.

```{r raw layerd plotting}
data("oneHunderdAddresses")

# Load spacial data for postcodes.
pc6 <- pollutionFromPc6(oneHunderdAddresses, "../../../data/cbs_pc6_2024.gpkg")
bag <- pollutionFromBag(oneHunderdAddresses, "../../../data/bag-light.gpkg")

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse$NO2FULL) + #Single layer
  geom_sf(data = pc6, aes(geometry = geom), fill = "purple", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = bag, aes(geometry = geom), colour = "orange") +
  scale_fill_grass_c(transform = "log10")
```

### Zooming and insetting
As discussed before the scale of ELAPSE prohibits proper visualization of the spatial data. PostcodElapse provides the helper function below to alleviate this:

- `geom_rectFeature()` Draws a rectangle around an set of spatial features.
- `coord_zoomFeature()` Zooms into a set of spatial features.

Together with ggpubr inset plots can be build, see the example below.

```{r raw inset plotting}
main <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse$NO2FULL) +
  geom_sf(data = pc6, aes(geometry = geom), fill = "purple", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = bag, aes(geometry = geom), colour = "orange") +
  scale_fill_grass_c(transform = "log10") +
  geom_rectFeature(pc6$geom[100], 5000) + # Annotate zoom location.
  labs(fill = bquote("log10 Concentration NO"[2]~"in µg/m"^3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
  
inset <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse$NO2FULL) +
  geom_sf(data = pc6, aes(geometry = geom), fill = "purple", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = bag, aes(geometry = geom), colour = "orange") +
  scale_fill_grass_c(transform = "log10") +
  coord_zoomFeature(pc6$geom[100]) # Zoom into postal address.

# Combine the two plots into a single figure.
fig <- ggarrange(main, inset,
  ncol = 2,
  common.legend = TRUE,
  legend.grob = get_legend(main)
)

# Label the figure
label <- 
"NO2 pollutant levels at postal code level in the Netherlands.
Purple areas are postal adrreses from PC6, orange dots are buildings from BAG."

annotate_figure(fig, 
  fig.lab.pos = "bottom.left",
  fig.lab = label
)
```

## Merging BAG and PC6

All previous examples handle BAG & PC6 as separate data.frames, this simplify's layering of differing data sources, The disadvantage of this approach, ggplot cannot add the data source to the legend. To fix this BAG & PC6 have to be merged into a single data.frame, the code below achieves this.

```{r merge BAG and PC6}

# Merge the postcodes and geometry from BAG and PC6 into a single data.frame
# You can keep the pollution data from both, unnecessary for this example.
bag_pc6_merge <- merge(
  bag |> select(postcode, geom),
  pc6 |> select(postcode, geom),
  by = "postcode", suffixes = c(".bag", ".pc6")
)

names(bag_pc6_merge) <- c("postcode", "BAG", "PC6")

head(bag_pc6_merge, 5)
```

### Insetting with proper legend

Below is the figure from: "Zooming and insetting" re-created using the merged data.frame with a proper legend added.

```{r plot merged spacial features}
# Pivot the data longer so a single geom_sf can be used.
bag_pc6_merge <- bag_pc6_merge |>
  pivot_longer(c(BAG, PC6), names_to = "gpkg", values_to = "geom")

# Re-create the plot
main <- ggplot(bag_pc6_merge) +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse$NO2FULL) +
  geom_sf(aes(geometry = geom, colour = gpkg), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_rectFeature(pc6$geom[100], 5000) +
  scale_fill_grass_c(transform = "log10") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("orange", "purple")) + # Apply the colours
  labs(
    fill = bquote("Log10 concentration NO"[2]~" in µg/m"^3),
    colour = "GeoPackage")+
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text = element_text(vjust = -1))

inset <- ggplot(bag_pc6_merge) +
  geom_spatraster(data = elapse$NO2FULL) +
  geom_sf(aes(geometry = geom, colour = gpkg), fill = NA, linewidth = 1) +
  coord_zoomFeature(pc6$geom[100]) +
  scale_fill_grass_c(transform = "log10") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("orange", "purple"))

fig <- ggarrange(main, inset,
                 ncol = 2,
                 common.legend = TRUE,
                 legend.grob = get_legend(main))

label <-
"NO2 pollutant levels at postal code level in the Netherlands. 
Postal coded geo-locations extracted from the BAG and PC6 GeoPackages."

annotate_figure(fig,
                fig.lab.pos = "bottom.left",
                fig.lab = label)
```
